crew_field_steps: Examine one raceme close up: green flattened spikelets alternate along the axis; purple flower parts project from several.
Differentiate purple protruding anthers/stigmas from seed awns; the seedhead is not a foxtail or purple flowering plume.
Before naming a variety or separating from P. pubiflorum/distichum, obtain leaf blade/hairiness, ligule, whole plant and mature measured spikelets.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Narrow racemes are not enough: compare wet-ground creeping P. distichum (often 2 branch V and TRUE rooted stolons) and P. pubiflorum (often several racemes and more robust 2.7–3.2 mm oval spikelets). Purple parts are anthers/stigmas, NOT purple grains. Record blade and sheath surface hairs by actual macro.
do_not_use_alone: Number of racemes without the entire flowering axis
Habitat, height, or vegetative tuft in isolation
Microscopic glume hairs or spikelet length inferred from a photo without scale

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Paspalum: what to inspect
steps: Use the paired flower macro and full raceme photo to teach head/flower organization; photograph same-plant foliage, ligule, maturity and glume traits with ruler before any variety ID.
First show the WHOLE head, then ONE one-sided raceme and attached spikelets. Never treat a photograph of one branch as total raceme count.
Obtain a real intact mature spikelet and measure it with 1-mm reference; use margin hair pattern and glumes to separate close Paspalum taxa.
Photograph blade/sheath joint and same-plant rootstock; knotgrass needs actually rooted horizontal stolons, not merely a low mat.
If plant photo is source-labelled only, keep identity tentative and leave existing county-native fields unchanged.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: P. setaceum often has one to few narrow racemes with relatively small spikelets and highly variable varieties differing in blade hairiness. Creeping wet-ground P. distichum typically has two terminal racemes and obvious stolons, while P. pubiflorum often has several racemes and larger spikelets. A single closeup of spikelets is not enough to prove variety.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Gross photo structures are references, NOT expert confirmation. Even new licensed images are PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING and not proof of Hays County presence.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.look_here_first: THIN PASPALUM: check a small, tufted or short-rhizomed perennial with one to a few terminal or sometimes axillary one-sided racemes; then verify PAIRED, flattened 1.4–2.6 mm spikelets and a very short (0.2–0.5 mm) membranous ligule. Purple exserted flower parts are anthers/stigmas, NOT awns. Leaf hairs vary among varieties; do not infer variety from one flowering photograph.

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Perennial, tufted or shortly rhizomatous; culms approximately 25–110 cm across FNA, often spreading or erect; no long rooted stolon mat like P. distichum.
measured_diagnostic_key.source: Flora of North America via NEON; Kew GrassBase

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Usually 1–2, sometimes up to 5–6; branches about 2–12(17) cm; axillary branches can remain partly enclosed in sheath.
measured_diagnostic_key.source: FNA via NEON; Kew POWO GrassBase

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Approximately 1.4–2.6 mm long, commonly paired, crowded in two rows on one side of raceme; plano-convex, with one sterile and one fertile floret.
Absent or obscure; do not label lower sterile lemma as a lower glume.
About spikelet-length (1.4–2.6 mm), three-veined, glabrous to minutely glandular-pubescent, with possible capitate hairs.
About spikelet-length, membranous, generally three-veined, smooth or minutely hairy; sterile palea absent or rudimentary.
Approximately 1.4–2.6 mm, hard/indurate, convex, involute margins, no true awn; paired fertile palea similarly hardened.
Very short true membrane 0.2–0.5 mm, with separate white hairs BEHIND membrane; hairs are not a replacement for membrane measurement.
measured_diagnostic_key.source: Go Botany; FNA via NEON; UMass

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Leaf blades variably glabrous or hairy, often papillose-ciliate along margin in some varieties; no variety assignment without actual same-plant hairs and mature spikelets.

crew_sequence: Find rooted crown and whole flowering culm; photograph terminal plus axillary racemes, including sheaths.
With hand lens, verify pairs of 1.4–2.6 mm spikelets along one side of raceme; separate purple anthers/stigmas from any glume/lemma structures.
Expose inner 0.2–0.5 mm membranous ligule with a 1-mm ruler and separately photograph hairs behind it.
Dissect mature spikelet: missing lower glume, upper three-veined glume, lower sterile lemma, hard upper fertile lemma; do not invent a long awn.
If variety-level hair characters or mature spikelets are unobservable, leave variety unassigned.

local_lookalikes.separation: Long rooted aboveground wet-ground stolons, usually V-shaped two racemes, typically larger 2.4–4 mm spikelets; head silhouette overlaps.
Often several racemes and larger roughly 2.7–3.2 mm spikelets in project key; compare same-scale ripe spikelets and upper-glume hairs.
Often several fingerlike racemes; compare spikelet arrangement, leaf hairs, ligule and perennial rootstock rather than foliage hairiness alone.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FEW NARROW RACEMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Usually one or two slender one-sided racemes, occasionally several; examine a whole flowering culm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Thin paspalum is a tufted or short-rhizomatous perennial, often 25–110 cm across treatments. Terminal and sometimes axillary racemes may be partly hidden in the leaf sheaths. Panels 1 and 3 show genuine flowering portions but not a rooted whole Texas plant. Do not assign a variety from a flowering branch alone. NEW gallery panel 5 (index4) now shows actual source-identified field-growing thin paspalum with basal green leaves and elongated fertile stems in their habitat, not just a cut seedhead. Its flowering stalks are among overlapping plants so one crown-to-head path is still somewhat obstructed; source observation belongs to botanist Alex Abair, Florida not Hays.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL FIELD-GROWING LEAFY TUFT PHOTO NOW COVERED — HAYS VOUCHER STILL OPEN

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · INNER TRUE LIGULE AND HAIR PLACEMENT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Very short membranous ligule about 0.2–0.5 mm; separate adjacent white hairs.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open the blade–sheath junction at 10–20× and measure the free membrane with a 1-mm reference. Leaf blade margins and sheaths may be variably hairy, including papillose-based hairs in some varieties; the source blade photograph cannot prove individual hair bases or the true membrane. Do not use hairiness alone to name a variety.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CALIBRATED TRUE LIGULE AND MARGIN HAIRS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · PAIRED MATURE SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Small, flattened spikelets about 1.4–2.6 mm, often in pairs along one side.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Inspect attached ripe spikelets at 10–20× with a millimeter scale. Each spikelet encloses one lower sterile and one upper fertile floret; two adjacent spikelets are not two florets. Purple protruding organs in panel 1 are anthers and stigmas, NOT purple seeds or awns. Current pictures do not establish calibrated spikelet length.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL FLOWERING SPIKELETS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO MEASURED MATURE PAIRS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · ABSENT LOWER GLUME; TWO DISTINCT LEMMAS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume absent or obscure; upper glume and sterile lemma thin; fertile lemma hard and awnless.
field_id_short_tiles.details: At 20–40× dissect one mature spikelet. The upper glume is approximately spikelet-length and usually three-veined; the lower sterile lemma is also thin and about spikelet-length. The upper fertile lemma is hardened with incurved margins and an enclosed palea. No long projecting lemma awn is expected. Fine hairs and glume veins must not be arrowed unless pixels resolve them.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · DISTICHUM AND PUBIFLORUM LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Thin paspalum: few racemes, small spikelets; knotgrass: rooted stolons; pubiflorum: often larger spikelets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Paspalum distichum commonly has two terminal racemes, spikelets about 2.4–4 mm and true rooted aboveground stolons in wet ground. P. pubiflorum often has several racemes and about 2.7–3.2 mm spikelets. Branch counts and size can overlap; verify actual rooted habit, mature spikelets and glume pubescence. Panel 2 is PUBIFLORUM, explicitly a different species. Avoid variety-level claims without same-plant foliage anatomy. NEW original large Dallisgrass CC BY-SA4 photographed 5mm spikelet plate (gallery panel6, index5) is explicitly another INTRODUCED species, while the existing P. pubiflorum (panel2,index1) is another differently identified grass. Compare little pale thin paspalum spikelets against larger silk-margined Dallisgrass, but glumes have NOT been dissected in P. setaceum.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ACTUAL TWO-TAXON COMPARISON PHOTO PAIR COVERED — MATCHED SIZE/GLUME DISSECTION MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE / TWO HANDOFFS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Four licensed local exact thin-paspalum JPEGs; true inner 0.2–0.5-mm membrane still missing.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Current actual photos in GitHub: FOUR physically archived target-species CC BY4 Alex Abair JPEGs including NEW naturally growing tuft and full culm image 49099738, macro of real paired pale spikelets with purple floral organs, source full raceme photo, and blade margin photo. Two different-species look-alike gallery panels: hairyseed paspalum iNat CC BY-NC conditional site-use verification and introduced Dallisgrass CC BY-SA4 author-scaled macro (locally hosted in Dallisgrass canonical folder).
